questions.questionText: A pretext may use a believable identity or story and rely on trust, empathy, or authority to persuade someone.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The lesson says believable stories and personas can exploit trust, empathy, authority, and urgency to gain cooperation.

questions.questionText: A caller you don't recognize asks you to send over sensitive corporate information, claiming it's urgently needed for a same-day audit. What is the gold standard rule for handling this kind of request?

options.text: Share the data if the caller sounds friendly.
Verify identity and authorization through official channels before releasing any data.
Always post data on public forums.
Never talk to anyone at work.

questions.explanation: Always verify identity and clearance before transmitting sensitive data.

questions.questionText: How do identity verification and documented procedures help reduce the risk of pretexting?

options.text: Allowing employees to share passwords freely.
They add checks that help confirm identity, authorization, and whether a request follows approved procedures.
Removing password locks from work laptops.
Disabling all antivirus software.

questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that verification and approved channels add checks that help protect confidential information; they do not guarantee that every pretext will be prevented.

questions.questionText: What distinguishes a pretext from a direct request that simply asks for information or access?

options.text: A pretext uses a believable identity or story to gain trust before requesting information or access.
A pretext is always sent to many people in a generic message.
A pretext is trustworthy whenever the person knows a coworker's name.
A pretext can only happen in a face-to-face conversation.

questions.explanation: The lesson defines pretexting as using a false identity or convincing story to gain trust and obtain information or access.

questions.questionText: How can an invented identity or story help a pretexter?

options.text: It proves the caller's identity without requiring verification
It can make the request seem believable and help the attacker gain trust
It confirms that a manager approved the request
It removes the need to follow the documented approval process

questions.explanation: The lesson explains that a false identity or believable story can gain trust before an attacker asks for sensitive information or access.

questions.questionText: Someone posing as a vendor pressures you to resolve their "urgent" access request directly with them instead of submitting an official IT service ticket. Why might a pretexter want to avoid the formal ticketing process?

options.text: A formal request is slower than sending a message
Skipping the established process may bypass identity checks and documented approval
A vendor is never allowed to submit an IT request
The request is automatically safe if it sounds urgent

questions.explanation: The lesson says urgency does not replace identity checks or documented approval; use the established process or an authorized exception path.

questions.questionText: The lesson's examples include remote administrators and workers handling HR, customer, or vendor information, not only executives.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The lesson identifies remote workers handling administrative data, HR workflows, customer records, and vendor management as its audience.

questions.questionText: A new vendor asks for a sample customer export to test its system, but Procurement has not confirmed the contract. What should you do?

options.text: Send the directory file immediately.
Do not send records; confirm the contract and approved data-sharing scope with Procurement before sharing anything.
Ask the vendor to pay you $50.
Send them dummy data containing real employee passwords.

questions.explanation: The lesson's new-vendor example says to confirm the contract and approved data-sharing scope because even sample files may contain sensitive information.

questions.questionText: Out-of-band verification is ineffective against pretexting.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Independent out-of-band verification effectively exposes pretexts by contacting the real organization or individual.

questions.questionText: A WhatsApp message from a new number claims to be a coworker who lost a phone and urgently asks you to forward a customer spreadsheet. What should you do?

options.text: Send the spreadsheet immediately because the coworker says it is urgent
Verify the person's identity through established work channels before sharing any records
Ask the new number to repeat the coworker's name before sending the spreadsheet
Forward the spreadsheet to a personal address supplied by the new number

questions.explanation: The lesson's coworker example uses an unknown WhatsApp number and a request for customer records; verify the person's identity through established work channels before sharing records.

questions.questionText: What is the primary characteristic of a pretexting attack?

options.text: Bombarding a website with fake internet traffic.
Fabricating a scenario and identity to build trust and trick a victim into sharing data.
Infecting USB drives left in public parking lots.
Sending mass generic spam to millions of emails.

questions.explanation: Pretexting centers on creating a plausible false persona and narrative.

questions.questionText: Pretexting attacks always happen within a single 30-second interaction and never involve multi-day conversations.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Pretexting often uses a "slow-burn" approach, building rapport across multiple days or weeks.

questions.questionText: An external auditor asks for an employee directory or software inventory and says an IT ticket will take too long. What should the worker do?

options.text: Send the requested information because the caller claims to be an auditor
Verify the auditor's identity and route the request through the approved internal process
Send a small sample first and verify the request afterward
Use a personal email address to avoid delaying the request

questions.explanation: The lesson's process-bypass guidance says to verify identity and authorization and not skip documented approval for an external request.

questions.questionText: Which of the following personas are common disguises used in pretexting campaigns? *(Select TWO)*

options.text: An external compliance auditor conducting an "urgent audit."
A new vendor asking for a sample customer-record export before Procurement confirms the contract.
An automated operating system update wizard.
A physical hardware firewall appliance.

questions.explanation: The lesson describes an external auditor requesting an employee directory and software inventory, and a new-vendor persona requesting a sample customer export before Procurement confirms the contract.

questions.questionText: A LinkedIn message claims to be from HR and uses a plausible job title. Does that alone prove the sender is genuine?

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The lesson's fictional LinkedIn HR example shows that a plausible title and friendly conversation do not verify identity or authorization.

questions.questionText: A pretext begins with casual conversation over several days before the attacker makes an unusual request. What is the attacker building during that time?

options.text: Buffer Overflow
Credibility and trust through a plausible persona and story
Man-in-the-Middle
Zero-Day Exploit

questions.explanation: The lesson explains that a pretext can build trust over time or unfold across days, but a friendly tone does not establish authorization.

questions.questionText: A remote contractor receives an email from someone claiming to be "Head of Global Security": *"We are running a silent security exercise. Do not inform your supervisor. Send your current VPN credentials directly to this email."* What should the contractor do?

options.text: Follow instructions and keep quiet.
Ignore the secrecy request and immediately report the message to their official supervisor and security team.
Reply asking for a cash reward.
Post the VPN credentials on an online forum.

questions.explanation: Demands for secrecy and credential submission are major red flags; legitimate security exercises do not collect user passwords via email.

questions.questionText: Which conversational signs suggest an interaction may be a pretexting attempt? *(Select TWO)*

options.text: The contact asks for confidential data while insisting you skip standard manager approval.
The contact uses an elaborate, emotional story to justify an unusual information request.
The contact directs you to submit a ticket through the official company portal.
The contact's identity is verified by your department manager in person.

questions.explanation: Bypassing procedures and using high-emotion stories are common pretexting tactics.

questions.questionText: An external auditor asks for employee home addresses. What should you do?

options.text: Send the addresses after the auditor repeats the request
Do not provide them; verify the request through a known HR contact and follow the approved process
Remove employee names but send the addresses to the external contact
Ask the auditor to confirm approval through the same message thread

questions.explanation: The lesson treats employee records as sensitive and directs workers to verify requests through established HR and approval channels.

questions.questionText: The lesson demonstrates pretexts through a LinkedIn HR message, a work-chat vendor request, and a WhatsApp coworker message.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Those examples show that an invented identity or story can appear in more than one communication channel; verify the person and their authorization.
